cf.title: Disallow whole-row index references with virtual generated columns?

input.subject: Disallow whole-row index references with virtual generated columns?

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection disputes the goal: message #3 shows a unique index that keys on (1,) while SQL returns (1,2). Two fixable design gaps remain. The check runs only in DefineIndex, so `alter table ... add column ... virtual` on a table with a whole-row index reaches the same state (replication-ondisk-1). The proposal also does not say what pg_upgrade or a restore does with indexes of this kind that already exist (standards-compat-1).

brief.title: Reject whole-row index references on tables with virtual generated columns
brief.problem: DefineIndex rejects virtual generated columns named directly in index expressions and predicates, but it accepts whole-row Vars that include them. Index build and maintenance evaluate against the physical heap tuple, where the virtual column is missing. So a whole-row expression index keys on (1,) while SQL sees (1,2), and a partial unique index with WHERE t IS NOT NULL can leave rows out and fail to enforce uniqueness.
brief.proposed_design: The patch extends the existing check in DefineIndex to reject whole-row Vars (varattno = 0) in index expressions and predicates when the relation has any virtual generated column. Whole-row references stay allowed on relations without virtual generated columns. The author calls this a conservative stopgap until RelationGetIndexExpressions() and RelationGetIndexPredicate() support virtual generated columns.
user_visible_surface: create index with a whole-row reference in an expression or a where predicate now raises an error when the table has a virtual generated column.
author_claims: A whole-row Var on such a relation bypasses the existing restriction on indexing virtual generated columns.
A whole-row expression index stores keys without the virtual column, for example (1,) where select returns (1,2).
A partial unique index with a whole-row predicate can silently skip rows and leave uniqueness unenforced.
Existing whole-row indexes on tables without virtual generated columns are not affected.
brief.thread_state: Álvaro Herrera questioned a virtual-column-specific fix and doubted the use of whole-row indexes; Matthias van de Meent showed STORED and VIRTUAL behave differently and suggested whole-row IS [NOT] NULL in indexes may be unsafe in general. The CF reviewer instead points to CF 5667, which adds index support for virtual generated columns, and nobody has reviewed this patch directly.
unclear: The material does not say what happens to existing indexes of this kind after upgrade, or whether pg_dump output will now fail to restore.
The material does not show the error message text or the error code.
The material does not say whether alter table add column of a virtual generated column, on a table that already has a whole-row index, is also rejected.
The thread does not say whether this fix should be dropped if CF 5667 is committed.
The thread does not settle Matthias's broader point that whole-row IS NOT NULL predicates break when columns are added.
search_queries: row IS NOT NULL index predicate

objections.title: Adding a virtual generated column later still creates the broken index
objections.failure_scenario: A user has `create unique index ... on t (a) where t is not null` on a table with no virtual column, which passes the new check. They then run `alter table t add column b int generated always as (a * 2) virtual`. The index now evaluates the predicate on the heap tuple without b, and uniqueness gaps appear exactly as in message #1.
objections.argument: The patch touches only indexcmds.c, so the check runs at DefineIndex time. The invariant the patch protects is that no index evaluates a whole-row value that is missing a virtual column. ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN reaches the same state without passing through DefineIndex. Matthias in message #4 already noted that adding columns can change whole-row IS NOT NULL results, so this path is known to matter.
objections.author_must_show: Does alter table add column of a virtual generated column fail when the table already has an index with a whole-row reference, and where is that enforced?

critic.reasoning: The patch touches only indexcmds.c, and alter table add column does not go through DefineIndex. The material does not say that this path is rejected, so the wrong-key state from message #3 stays reachable.

objections.title: Existing whole-row indexes on such tables block dump restore and pg_upgrade
objections.failure_scenario: A Postgres 18 user has a whole-row expression or partial index on a table with a virtual generated column. pg_upgrade to 19 replays that CREATE INDEX from the schema dump, the new check rejects it, and the upgrade stops partway. A plain pg_dump restore also fails at that index, and the user learns this only during the restore.
objections.argument: Virtual generated columns already shipped, so these indexes can exist in the field today, and the patch is tagged Bugfix. The proposal does not mention upgrade, restore, or a pg_upgrade pre-check. Message #1 says existing whole-row indexes "should not be affected", but that covers only tables without virtual generated columns. If the fix is back-patched, a minor release would also start rejecting a dump that the same major version produced.
objections.author_must_show: What does pg_upgrade or a restore do with an existing index of this kind, and should pg_upgrade --check report it before the upgrade starts?

critic.reasoning: Virtual generated columns shipped in 18 and DefineIndex accepts these indexes today, so they can exist in the field. The proposal does not say how pg_upgrade or a restore handles them, and the thread does not discuss it.

refuted.title: Adding a virtual generated column later bypasses the new check
refuted.failure_scenario: A user creates a table with a whole-row partial unique index, then runs alter table t add column b int generated always as (a * 2) virtual. The index now evaluates its predicate against heap tuples that lack b. Uniqueness goes unenforced as in message #1, and nothing reports an error.
refuted.argument: The patch puts the check only in DefineIndex, and the commit message lists only indexcmds.c. Adding a column through ALTER TABLE reaches the same broken state without going through DefineIndex. Message #4 makes a related point about whole-row IS NOT NULL predicates when columns are added, so the gap is real and was not settled in the thread.
refuted.author_must_show: Does alter table add column of a virtual generated column fail when a whole-row index exists, and if not, how is that state prevented?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1, which states the same alter table path under the safety item.

refuted.title: Existing indexes break pg_upgrade and dump restore with no prior check
refuted.failure_scenario: A PG18 cluster has a whole-row expression index on a table with a virtual column. pg_upgrade to 19 restores the schema with the new server, the `create index` fails, and the upgrade stops late in the process. A plain pg_dump restore fails in the same way.
refuted.argument: Virtual generated columns shipped in 18, so such indexes can exist in the field today. The proposal adds a new error but does not say what pg_upgrade checks for, or what a user should do with an index that is already wrong. The CF entry tags this as a bugfix. If it is backpatched, a minor release would also make restore of dumps from the same major version fail.
refuted.author_must_show: Will pg_upgrade detect these indexes in its check phase and report them, and what is the recommended fix for users of 18 who already have one?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. Its extra question about the recommended fix for users of 18 belongs with that objection.

refuted.title: Check at create index only; alter table add column is not covered
refuted.failure_scenario: A user creates a unique index on (t) or with WHERE t IS NOT NULL on a table with no virtual columns, which the patch allows. Later they run alter table add column b int generated always as (a * 2) virtual. The index now has the same wrong keys and the same missing uniqueness enforcement, and nothing reports an error.
refuted.argument: The patch touches only indexcmds.c, so the new rule lives in DefineIndex alone. The invariant it protects is "no index reads a virtual column", and a later alter table can break that invariant on an existing index. Each path that adds a virtual column to a table that already has indexes would need the same check, and a future patch that misses one fails silently. The proposal does not say whether alter table is rejected or left open.
refuted.author_must_show: What happens when a virtual generated column is added to a table that already has a whole-row expression index or whole-row predicate?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1. The maintainability framing adds no separate failure beyond the same alter table add column gap.

refuted.title: Stopgap overlaps CF 5667, which removes the same restriction
refuted.failure_scenario: The committer takes this patch, and CF 5667 then adds index support for virtual generated columns. The whole-row check must be found and taken out or rewritten in the same release. If it stays, users get an error for indexes the new code supports correctly.
refuted.argument: Message #3 calls the patch a stopgap until RelationGetIndexExpressions() and RelationGetIndexPredicate() handle virtual columns. Messages #6 and #7 point to CF 5667, which claims to do that and shows whole-row predicate indexes enforcing uniqueness. The thread has no agreement on which patch goes first or whether this one is dropped if 5667 lands. Without that, two patches change the same rule in opposite directions.
refuted.author_must_show: Is this patch meant for back branches only, and does it become unnecessary or conflicting once CF 5667 is committed?

critic.reasoning: The new check extends the existing virtual-column check in DefineIndex, which CF 5667 must remove anyway, so no extra hidden cleanup arises. A removable error check is not a permanent commitment, and released branches need a fix that a feature patch cannot provide.

refuted.title: New error can make existing dumps fail to restore
refuted.failure_scenario: A user on a release with virtual generated columns already has a whole-row index on such a table. After a minor update with this fix, or a dump and restore into 19, the create index in the dump fails. pg_upgrade may fail the same way, and the user finds out during the upgrade.
refuted.argument: The CF entry tags this as a bugfix. Virtual generated columns already shipped, so such indexes can exist today. The proposal does not say what happens to them or whether the fix is backpatched. A committer would likely ask for the upgrade path before adding a new create index error in a back branch.
refuted.author_must_show: How do users with an existing whole-row index on a table with virtual columns get through pg_dump restore and pg_upgrade after this change?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which covers the same restore and pg_upgrade failure, including the back-patch case.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: pg_upgrade replays create index for existing whole-row indexes on tables with virtual generated columns, and the new check rejects them.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: see objection replication-ondisk-1: Adding a virtual generated column later still creates the broken index

touch_points.label: pg_dump / restore round-trip
touch_points.reason: A dump that contains such an index fails to restore at the create index statement.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The CF entry is tagged Bugfix and virtual generated columns already shipped, so a back-patch would add a new create index error in a minor release.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The check must be removed or rewritten when index support for virtual generated columns arrives, as message #3 says.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Does `alter table ... add column ... generated always as (...) virtual` fail when the table already has an index with a whole-row reference, and where is that enforced?
What do pg_upgrade and a pg_dump restore do with an existing index of this kind, and should pg_upgrade --check report it?
Is the fix meant for back branches, and what should users who already have such an index do?
If CF 5667 is committed, is this patch dropped for master and kept for released branches only?
Does the patch address Matthias's point that whole-row IS [NOT] NULL predicates in indexes may be unsafe on any table when columns are added?

committability.owner_note: Álvaro Herrera replied in message #2 but questioned the virtual-column-specific scope and did not offer to take the patch. The owner needs to know DefineIndex and the generated-column code.
committability.liability: A new create index error, possibly in a released branch, and the restore and pg_upgrade failures it can cause for existing indexes. The check must be removed when index support for virtual generated columns arrives.
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered the first review the same day in message #3, with new test cases.

priority.reason: The patch is 4.3 KB in indexcmds.c plus regression tests, and it affects only whole-row indexes on tables with virtual generated columns. It fixes a silent uniqueness failure, but the alter table path and the upgrade path need an answer first.

provisional_note: Without the code, I could not check whether the check catches every form of whole-row reference, or whether alter table add column already rejects this case elsewhere. The error message and error code are also not shown.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
Reverted commit(s): Ensure that RowExprs and whole-row Vars produce the expected column names.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit bf7ca1587, I had the bright idea that we could make the
result of a whole-row Var (that is, foo.*) track any column aliases
that had been applied to the FROM entry the Var refers to.  However,
that's not terribly logically consistent, because now the output of
the Var is no longer of the named composite type that the Var claims
to emit.  bf7ca1587 tried to handle that by changing the output
tuple values to be labeled with a blessed RECORD type, but that's
really pretty disastrous: we can wind up storing such tuples onto
disk, whereupon they're not readable by other sessions.

The only practical fix I can see is to give up on what bf7ca1587
tried to do, and say that the column names of tuples produced by
a whole-row Var are always those of the underlying named composite
type, query aliases or no.  While this introduces some inconsistencies,
it removes others, so it's not that awful in the abstract.  What *is*
kind of awful is to make such a behavioral change in a back-patched
bug fix.  But corrupt data is worse, so back-patched it will be.

(A workaround available to anyone who's unhappy about this is to
introduce an extra level of sub-SELECT, so that the whole-row Var is
referring to the sub-SELECT's output and not to a named table type.
Then the Var is of type RECORD to begin with and there's no issue.)

Per report from Miles Delahunty.  The faulty commit dates to 9.5,
so back-patch to all supported branches.

precedents_retrieved.title: DOCS for generated column replication
precedents_retrieved.summary: Peter Smith proposed an "Examples" subsection for the new "Generated Column Replication" documentation page. The patch adds a few self-contained publication and subscription examples, including one showing that a publication column list overrides publish_generated_columns.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila judged the current text and example sufficient, and preferred to wait for user feedback on the new feature before adding more examples. No one else supported the patch, so vignesh C closed the entry for lack of interest, open to revisit if users ask for it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This is a new feature, and I think it is better to
get some feedback from users. We can add more examples or information
based on real user feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: COPY WHERE clause generated/system column reference
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patches make COPY FROM ... WHERE work with generated columns: they expand virtual generated columns in the WHERE clause and compute stored generated columns before the WHERE clause is checked. They also reject system columns other than tableoid in the WHERE clause.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut committed a smaller fix that rejects generated columns in COPY FROM WHERE with a clear error, and left tableoid for a separate thread. He then argued that support should not be added, because generated columns belong to the target table while the WHERE clause filters input data. Masahiko Sawada had shown that computing stored generated columns before the WHERE clause runs them before BEFORE INSERT triggers, so the WHERE clause changes the row the trigger sees.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This seems fundamentally wrong, because generated columns are a
property of the target table, but the COPY WHERE clause is meant to
filter the input data.

precedents_retrieved.title: generated columns
precedents_retrieved.summary: Peter Eisentraut proposed implementing SQL-standard generated columns (GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr)), with the generation expression stored in pg_attrdef like a default and MySQL/Oracle-style VIRTUAL|STORED syntax. Only the VIRTUAL (computed-on-read) variant was fully implemented; STORED, various ALTER TABLE forms and index support were deferred.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Review by Jaime Casanova found multiple bugs: generated columns showed no value through a view, inheritance produced a malformed default and a server crash on insert, ALTER COLUMN TYPE on the referenced or generated column failed with internal errors, triggers saw NULL for the generated column, and the generation expression could be dropped via DROP DEFAULT. Based on these reviews, the commitfest manager marked the entry Returned with feedback, asking for an updated version to be resubmitted.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Based on this review, and the errors noted in upthread in the previous review,
I’m marking this Returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow logical decoding to output generated columns
precedents_retrieved.authors: Peter Smith (smithpb2250), Shubham Khanna (skhanna), Shlok Kyal (shlokkyal)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Let pgoutput send generated column values in logical replication, so consumers get a complete row instead of computing generated columns on the subscriber. The work added replication of generated columns named in a publication column list, then a publish_generated_columns publication parameter.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Most of the work was committed before the entry closed: generated columns in column lists and the publish_generated_columns parameter. After that commit, Peter Eisentraut asked how the feature should work with the proposed virtual generated columns, which he thought could not be replicated, and Amit Kapila suggested limiting the option to stored generated columns. The thread then went idle in Waiting on Author, and Michael Paquier returned the entry until that question is settled.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: As of now this thread is just waiting on author and idle in the CF app for no real purpose.

precedents_retrieved.title: plpgsql - possibility to get element or array type for referenced variable type
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets PL/pgSQL `%TYPE` refer to variables of composite type, including polymorphic parameters. It also adds syntax to derive the array type or the element type of a referenced variable, first as `%ARRAYTYPE`/`%ELEMENTTYPE` and later as `%TYPE[]` and `ELEMENT OF ...%TYPE`.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane proposed rejecting this PL/pgSQL-only implementation. He wanted these type operators added to the core grammar's Typename production, so PL/pgSQL would pick them up automatically. Joe Conway and Jim Nasby agreed. The author then found that a reduced patch with only the composite `%TYPE` fix gave too little benefit, and asked for it to be rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I played with the reduced patch, and the benefit without all other things
is negligible. It should be rejected.

precedents_retrieved.title: allow mix of composite and scalar variables in target list
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the PL/pgSQL parser check that rejects a row (composite) variable inside a multiple-item INTO list. With several targets, each target would take one output column, so a composite variable would receive one composite-valued column; record variables were left out.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that this makes a row variable mean one column in a multi-item INTO list but one column per field when it is the only target. That inconsistency would also limit later changes for backward-compatibility reasons. He asked for new notation that removes the ambiguity, and Robert Haas's support for the 1:1 matching did not settle it. The CF manager moved the patch on as needing a revised version, and Pavel Stehule answered with two new design options.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm fine with doing something where we add new notation to dispel
the ambiguity.  I don't want to put in another layer of inconsistency
and then have even more backwards-compatibility problems constraining
our response to the inevitable complaints.

precedents_retrieved.title: Predicate locking in Gin index
precedents_retrieved.summary: A GSoC 2017 patch adding explicit predicate locking to the GIN index access method for serializable isolation, placing page-level predicate locks on entry tree and posting tree leaf pages and copying locks on page splits. It also handled conflict detection when fast update is enabled.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewer Alexander Korotkov found the locking scheme redundant and asked for changes: lock posting tree leaves instead of entry tree leaves, apply page-level locks only when fast update is off, add in-code comments, and improve the isolation tests so they actually create posting trees. After his last review the thread had no updates for almost two months, and Michael Paquier marked the entry returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix index-only scan plans, take 2.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Fix index-only scan plans, take 2.
Reverted commit(s): Fix index-only scan plans when not all index columns can be returned.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 4ace45677 failed to fix the problem fully, because the
same issue of attempting to fetch a non-returnable index column
can occur when rechecking the indexqual after using a lossy index
operator.  Moreover, it broke EXPLAIN for such indexquals (which
indicates a gap in our test cases :-().

Revert the code changes of 4ace45677 in favor of adding a new field
to struct IndexOnlyScan, containing a version of the indexqual that
can be executed against the index-returned tuple without using any
non-returnable columns.  (The restrictions imposed by check_index_only
guarantee this is possible, although we may have to recompute indexed
expressions.)  Support construction of that during setrefs.c
processing by marking IndexOnlyScan.indextlist entries as resjunk
if they can't be returned, rather than removing them entirely.
(We could alternatively require setrefs.c to look up the IndexOptInfo
again, but abusing resjunk this way seems like a reasonably safe way
to avoid needing to do that.)

This solution isn't great from an API-stability standpoint: if there
are any extensions out there that build IndexOnlyScan structs directly,
they'll be broken in the next minor releases.  However, only a very
invasive extension would be likely to do such a thing.  There's no
change in the Path representation, so typical planner extensions
shouldn't have a problem.

As before, back-patch to all supported branches.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert GetTransactionSnapshot() to return historic snapshot during LR
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert GetTransactionSnapshot() to return historic snapshot during LR
Reverted commit(s): Don't allow GetTransactionSnapshot() in logical decoding
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 1585ff7387 changed GetTransactionSnapshot() to throw an error
if it's called during logical decoding, instead of returning the
historic snapshot. I made that change for extra protection, because a
historic snapshot can only be used to access catalog tables while
GetTransactionSnapshot() is usually called when you're executing
arbitrary queries. You might get very subtle visibility problems if
you tried to use the historic snapshot for arbitrary queries.

There's no built-in code in PostgreSQL that calls
GetTransactionSnapshot() during logical decoding, but it turns out
that the pglogical extension does just that, to evaluate row filter
expressions. You would get weird results if the row filter runs
arbitrary queries, but it is sane as long as you don't access any
non-catalog tables. Even though there are no checks to enforce that in
pglogical, a typical row filter expression does not access any tables
and works fine. Accessing tables marked with the user_catalog_table =
true option is also OK.

To fix pglogical with row filters, and any other extensions that might
do similar things, revert GetTransactionSnapshot() to return a
historic snapshot during logical decoding.

To try to still catch the unsafe usage of historic snapshots, add
checks in heap_beginscan() and index_beginscan() to complain if you
try to use a historic snapshot to scan a non-catalog table. We're very
close to the version 18 release however, so add those new checks only
in master.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. [P3] shares only the generated-column topic, and its reason, that the COPY WHERE clause filters input data while generated columns belong to the target table, does not apply to index definitions. The thread names no earlier attempt at this fix; message #7 points to CF 5667, which is a parallel proposal to add support rather than an earlier rejection.
The SQL surface is a new error on create index and adds no syntax, so no SQL standard conflict appears.

Two objections from the persistence angle. The new error adds no WAL, catalog or wire changes. The risks are a gap in the check, which ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN can bypass, and existing indexes that will not restore.

The proposal only adds an error in create index, and only the table owner can create the indexes it affects. The wrong keys and the unenforced uniqueness in messages #1 and #3 are data-integrity issues on the owner's own table, and no other role gains access or visibility through them. Nothing here changes privileges, defaults, authentication or exposure, so the security angle has no objection.
The cost for users who do not use the feature looks negligible: one extra check at create index time, and no hot-path or ABI impact.

Postgres has no existing feature that stops a whole-row index on a table with a virtual generated column from storing keys without that column. The proposal extends the check DefineIndex already makes, so it adds no second mechanism. CF 5667 is an uncommitted alternative and does not already meet the need. The workarounds in message #2 (IS DISTINCT FROM NULL, or a STORED column) avoid the bug but do not prevent it.

The patch is a bugfix, so demand is not the right test. Message #3 shows a unique index that stores keys without the virtual column, and a partial unique index that lets duplicate rows in without any error. Álvaro's doubt in message #5 that whole-row indexes have real users counts in favour of the restriction, because few users would hit the new error. Whether this fix or CF 5667 should go in is a design question for other angles.
